title: Agent architecture: an introduction
learner_summary: An engineering junior at a university who has written Python for classes (functions, lists and dicts, reading JSON, calling a web API in one class project) and has used a chatbot for homework help, but has never built an agent or called a language model from code. They want to build an assistant for their senior design project: a helper for the university makerspace that answers students' questions from the machine manuals, checks the booking calendar and books equipment time. They have had two short sessions so far, one on what a language model does and one on the agent loop, and have heard the words token and context window without knowing what they limit.

objectives.text: Describe the agent loop: a model, a set of tools and an environment that returns results, repeated until a stopping condition is met.
Explain tool calling: a tool is a described function that the model asks the program to run, and the program runs it and returns the result to the model.
Explain context and memory in an agent: the context window, what is kept between steps and between sessions, and retrieval and notes as memory.
Tell workflows and agents apart by who owns the control flow, and decide when a fixed workflow is the better choice.
Describe multi-agent systems: an orchestrator and workers with separate contexts, the benefits and the costs, and when not to use them.

facts.text: An agent runs in a loop: the model chooses an action, the program carries it out in the environment, and the result is given back to the model before it chooses the next action.
The environment is whatever the agent acts on and observes, such as files, a database, a web service or a running program; what it returns after an action is the agent's observation.
The model does not run continuously: each pass through the loop is a new, separate call to the model, and nothing happens inside the model between calls.

The loop ends on a stopping condition: normally when the model gives a final answer instead of requesting an action (in some designs, by calling a special finish action), and, as a safeguard, when a limit on steps, time or cost is reached.

Feedback from the environment, such as an error message or a failing test, is the most reliable way for an agent to detect and correct its mistakes; a loop with no outside check can repeat a mistake or stop with a wrong answer that it presents as right.
A tool is given to the model as a description: a name, a plain-language explanation of what it does, and a schema of the parameters it takes.
The model never executes a tool: it outputs a structured request naming the tool and its arguments, and software outside the model, usually the program that calls it, runs the tool.
After running a tool, the program sends the result, or the error if the tool failed, back to the model as part of the input to its next call.

The model learns what a tool does and how to call it from its input, mainly the tool's description, and not from the tool's code, which it normally never sees, so a vague or misleading description leads to wrong or missed calls.
When the program carries out a tool call itself, it can check, restrict or refuse the request before running it, for example by asking a person to approve an action that deletes or sends something.

The context window is the limit, counted in tokens, on how much the model can handle in one call, and everything in that call counts against it, such as the instructions, the tool descriptions, the conversation history, the tool results and the model's own reply.

The model itself keeps nothing from one call to the next: at every step the software around it must supply the history the model should use, and anything from earlier steps that is left out of that input is unknown to the model at that step.
Because the history grows with every step, a long-running agent has to manage its context, for example by summarizing earlier steps or dropping old tool results it no longer needs.

A larger context window does not remove the need to manage context: everything kept in the context is part of the input to every call and adds to that call's time and cost (caching can make repeated parts cheaper, but not free), and models tend to use details buried in a long context less reliably than the same details in a short one.

Nothing carries over from one session to the next unless it was saved outside the model, for example as notes the agent writes to a file or a database (a plan, decisions, facts about the user), and put back into the context in the new session.
Retrieval lets an agent use material too large to load whole, such as long manuals or a large store of saved notes: it searches that material and brings only the relevant parts into the context.

The difference between a workflow and an agent is who controls the order of steps: in a workflow, the programmer's code sets the steps and calls the model at fixed points; in an agent, the model chooses each next step while it runs.
A fixed workflow is the better choice when the steps, or the few paths between them, are known in advance, because it is more predictable, usually cheaper and easier to test than an agent.
An agent can be worth its extra cost when the right steps cannot be known in advance, for example when what to do next depends on what the last action revealed.
Because an agent chooses its own path, two runs on the same input can take different steps and different numbers of model calls, which makes its cost and behavior harder to predict and to test.
Workflows and agents can be combined: a workflow can include an agent as one of its steps, and an agent can be given a fixed workflow as one of its tools.
A sound way to choose is to start with the simplest design that works, such as a single model call or a fixed workflow, and to add autonomy only where tests show the simpler design failing.
In an orchestrator-worker system, one agent, the orchestrator, splits a task into subtasks, hands each one to a worker agent, and combines the workers' results.

In the usual orchestrator-worker design, each worker has its own separate context: it starts from the task description the orchestrator writes for it rather than from the orchestrator's history, and only the result it returns goes back into the orchestrator's context.
Splitting work across agents helps most when the subtasks are independent: the workers can run in parallel, and each one works in a short, focused context instead of one crowded context.

A multi-agent system usually uses more model calls and tokens than a single agent on the same task, because each worker needs its own instructions and context and the orchestrator must plan the split and combine the results.

Each hand-off can lose or distort information, because a worker that starts from a task description knows about the task only what that description tells it; vague or incomplete task descriptions are a common cause of multi-agent failures.
A single agent is usually the better choice when the steps depend closely on each other or share changing state, or when the whole task fits comfortably in one context.

misconceptions.text: An agent is just a chatbot with a longer or better prompt.
misconceptions.correction: What makes an agent is the loop: the actions the model asks for are carried out by the program, and the results come back to the model for its next step, until a stopping condition. A better prompt can improve a single answer, but it does not let the model act or see what its actions did.

misconceptions.text: More agents always give better results.
misconceptions.correction: Each extra agent adds model calls, tokens, time and hand-offs where information can be lost. Several agents help mainly when the work splits into independent parts; for small or tightly connected tasks, one agent usually does as well or better for less.

misconceptions.text: The model remembers earlier sessions on its own.
misconceptions.correction: The model keeps nothing between calls or between sessions. Anything an assistant seems to remember from an earlier session was saved outside the model, in a file or a database, and put back into the model's input by the software around it.

misconceptions.text: The model runs the tools itself.
misconceptions.correction: The model only writes a request that names a tool and its arguments. Software outside the model, usually the program around it, runs the tool and sends the result back, which is also where the program can check or block a request.

misconceptions.text: A big enough context window means you never have to think about what goes into it.
misconceptions.correction: Everything kept in the context is part of the input to every call and adds to its time and cost, and models tend to use details buried in a long, cluttered context less reliably. Long tasks can still need summarizing, dropping old results, notes or retrieval.

misconceptions.text: An agent left to run long enough will always get there, so it needs no stopping condition or outside feedback.
misconceptions.correction: Without feedback from the environment, such as test results or error messages, an agent can repeat the same mistake indefinitely or stop at a wrong answer. It needs that feedback to correct itself reliably, and a stopping condition, such as a final answer or a limit on steps or cost, to end the loop.
